items.claim: Seeing a %0d%0a payload echoed back in an HTML error page or response body is not CRLF injection: the flaw requires the injected CR and LF to become additional header field lines in the response, which the server's HTTP serializer, not the template engine, controls.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the reflected value is later re-emitted through a header-emitting API — for example the payload is stored and replayed by a Location or Set-Cookie header, or a downstream proxy/CDN re-serializes the stored value into a response header — in which case the body reflection is the first observable step of real header injection.

items.claim: CRLF injection is proved only by the raw response containing a header block the attacker controls — an extra header line, a truncated earlier header, or a second response head after the injected blank line — visible in a byte-level or non-normalising client view, not by a 200 status with attacker text in it.
items.disproof: The claim is false if the client used transparently normalises or de-duplicates repeated header fields (many HTTP libraries fold duplicates into a comma list), in which case the injection genuinely occurred but the evidence must come from a raw socket capture or a Wireshark/mitmproxy view rather than the library's parsed headers.

items.claim: Modern language-level header setters defeat naive CRLF payloads without any application sanitiser, because a value containing CR or LF raises a TypeError instead of being serialised, so a payload that is not percent-decoded twice and not split-and-rejoined before reaching the setter cannot inject a header.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the value is passed through a path that bypasses the guarded setter — a raw write to the socket, a C library or framework API that takes a pre-built header block, a template or config file that emits headers, or a reverse proxy that re-serialises a stored value — because those paths re-introduce the injection the TypeError was meant to prevent.

items.claim: The convincing CRLF evidence is a stored value containing a literal carriage-return/line-feed pair that reappears in a replayed header line, which distinguishes a genuine finding from the far more common case of a header value containing only percent-encoded %0d%0a that the server never decoded.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the application performs a single decode of the stored value immediately before header construction — then a percent-encoded payload in the submitted input still produces literal CRLF on the wire, and the encoded form alone is sufficient evidence provided the decode step is shown.

items.claim: A 3xx response whose Location value merely contains attacker-chosen text or an encoded newline is not CRLF injection: in several mainstream languages setting a Location header automatically produces the redirect status, so the status code is evidence of the redirect and not of an injected header line.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the Location value reaches the wire with a real CR/LF pair split into an additional header line, or when the redirect is emitted by a different component (a proxy, a CDN edge function, a web-server rewrite rule) than the one whose setter the tester assumed was sanitising the value.
